why: The pawn on d4 was attacked and undefended, and Bxd4 simply won it.
Castling ignored the knight fork on e2 and the Qxe4+ threat; Nc3 covered both.
Taking the g5 pawn with the knight removed the e6 defender of g7 and allowed Bxg7 mate.
Grabbing on d4 let White gain time with e5 hitting the bishop while Nxe4 was the better move.
Qxa5 won the loose queen, but the player took a pawn on d7 and left the rook to take over.
Nh3 allowed Nd4 and Nxc2+ forking king and rook while the king sat uncastled in the centre.
Recapturing on d4 left the e4 pawn undefended; e5 kept it safe and attacked d6.
The Bxf7+ threat was ignored, and the pinned f7 pawn could not be held while Rxe3 won a pawn.
f5 opened lines against the uncastled king and allowed Qh5+; Qc8 would have defended.
Taking on b6 ignored the Rxa2 threat that puts a rook on the seventh; a3 stopped it.
a5 ignored the Bh2+ and knight checks; g3 gave the king luft and avoided the perpetual.
The queen on g7 was pinned along the g-file and attacked twice; Qxe5 simply won a pawn safely.
Moving the b-pawn opened the d6-a3 diagonal and left the knight on a3 hanging; Nxb5 was available.
Capturing on d5 with the queen met a defender and lost it; Ra6 was the safe answer to the Qxb7 threat.
h3 attacks the bishop on g4 and gains time; d3 let Nd4 hit the queen with tempo.
